claim: If a return is filed on time but the tax is not paid in full, PA imposes a flat 5 percent 'underpayment penalty' on the unpaid balance after the original due date. It is a one-time 5%, not a monthly rate. The PA-40 instructions tie it to negligence or intentional disregard of rules without intent to defraud, which is 72 P.S. 7352(b)(1) (5%). A separate 25% penalty applies when unreported income exceeds 25% of the income shown (7352(b)(2)), and fraud is 50% (7352(c)). A check or EFT that bounces costs 10% of its face amount, at least $25 and at most $100.
establishes: PA's own PIT Guide, confirmed by the 2025 PA-40 instructions p.42 (https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/revenue/documents/formsandpublications/formsforindividuals/pit/documents/2025/2025_pa-40in.pdf): 'If you do not pay the full amount of your tax due with your extension or your timely filed return, PA law imposes a 5 percent underpayment penalty.'
uncertainty: No minimum is stated for the underpayment penalty. 72 P.S. 7352 has no provision titled failure to pay. The department's reliance on 7352(b)(1) comes from the PA-40 instructions. The 7352 text was read on FindLaw (https://codes.findlaw.com/pa/title-72-ps-taxation-and-fiscal-affairs/pa-st-sect-72-7352/), a secondary host, not the official PA site.
designImplication: Model PA late payment as a single 5% add-on when tax is unpaid at the due date. It does not grow with time; interest does the growing.

claim: Failure to file by the due date or extended due date: 5% of the tax required to be shown for the first month, plus 5% for each additional month or fraction, not exceeding 25% in the aggregate, and never less than $5, unless the delay had reasonable cause. The department 'may assess both late filing and underpayment penalties' when a return is filed late and the tax is not paid with it ('If you do not pay the liability when filing your late return, an additional 5 percent underpayment penalty will be imposed'). No combined cap is stated.
sourceDate: statute marked current as of 2026-01-01 by FindLaw; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: 72 P.S. 7352(a) rate, cap and $5 minimum. The same figures are on the department's PIT Guide page and in the 2025 PA-40 instructions p.42.
uncertainty: The 30% combined maximum (25% + 5%) is inferred from the two penalties being additive; no source states that number. The statute was read on FindLaw (secondary host); its figures match the department's own pages.
designImplication: Late filing in PA can cost 25% plus a flat 5%. The PA-40 instructions say it is better to file on time and pay 5% plus interest than not file and face up to 25%.

claim: Interest is simple and calculated daily: INTEREST = LATE OR UNPAID TAX x NUMBER OF DAYS x APPLICABLE DAILY INTEREST RATE. The rate is 7% a year (daily 0.000192), charged 1/1/25 to 12/31/26; 2024 was 8% (0.000219). The rate is the one the U.S. Secretary of the Treasury has in effect on January 1, and it stays fixed for the calendar year. Interest runs from the original due date to the date of payment. An extension does not stop it.
establishes: REV-1611 sets the 2026 rate, the daily factor and the formula. The PIT Guide says 'simple interest will be calculated daily from the date the tax is due to the date of payment'.
uncertainty: runsOnPenalties=false is read from the REV-1611 formula, which multiplies 'late or unpaid tax' only. No page says outright that penalties bear no interest. The 7% overpayment rate for 2026 comes from a Bloomberg Tax headline (secondary).
designImplication: PA interest: 7% simple on the unpaid tax only, accrued daily at 0.000192. Penalties do not grow.

claim: Individuals set up PIT payment plans through myPATH. A 'standard' plan is for a balance under $50,000 paid in under 12 months. An 'extended' plan is needed if the balance is $50,000 or more, the plan needs more than 12 months, or the taxpayer already has a payment plan with the department. An extended plan requires a REV-488 Statement of Financial Condition for Individuals. All previous returns must be filed first. REV-638 (Official Appeal Waiver Letter) brings in balances not yet in collections. The page says 'If you don't hear back within 48 hours, please check your spam and/or junk folder.' That refers to an email reply, not a decision deadline.

value.newBalanceWhileOnPlan: existing plan holders must apply for an extended plan

establishes: The $50,000 and 12-month thresholds for a self-service plan, the REV-488 requirement, the returns-filed precondition, and that an existing plan routes a new request to the extended plan.
uncertainty: Fee: NOT FOUND (none mentioned). Maximum term and balance for extended plans: NOT FOUND. Decision time: NOT FOUND (the 48 hours is tied to email only). autoDebitRequired comes from a search-engine summary of the department's FAQ site (revenue-pa.custhelp.com), which blocked direct fetching.
designImplication: PA: self-service plan if under $50k and under 12 months; anything bigger needs financial disclosure. A new balance while on a plan reopens the negotiation as an extended plan rather than joining silently.

claim: No official PA page found states what a missed plan payment does, whether there is a cure period, or whether refunds are held during a plan. The PA-40 instructions say the department 'will apply your overpayment to any outstanding PA personal income tax liability from a previous tax year', with no exception for balances on a plan. A search-engine excerpt of the department's FAQ says a plan 'will not preclude additional collection efforts through the Treasury Offset Program'. The department's wage-garnishment page says: 'Once a garnishment order is issued, a payment plan will no longer be an option.'
establishes: That a garnishment order ends plan eligibility (official). That state refunds go to prior PIT liabilities (2025 PA-40 instructions p.24, official).
uncertainty: Missed-payment effect and cure period: NOT FOUND on official sources. Secondary tax-relief sites (taxcure.com, gettaxreliefnow.com) say a missed payment or an unfiled new return defaults the plan and enforcement resumes. That is not used as a value. refundsOffsetDuringPlan is inferred from the unconditional PA-40 offset language. federalTOPDuringPlan rests on a search excerpt of a revenue-pa.custhelp.com answer, which could not be fetched directly.
designImplication: Treat PA plan default mechanics as unknown. Refunds keep paying down the debt during a plan.

claim: (1) A Billing Notice gives 30 days to respond. (2) A Notice of Assessment can be appealed to the Board of Appeals within 90 days for PIT (extended from 60 days effective 2025-01-27). It is final after that. (3) A Notice of Delinquency and other collection contact follow. (4) A Notice of Intent to Offset gives 60 days to pay before the debt goes to the IRS for federal refund offset. (5) A lien is filed with the county Prothonotary, and the taxpayer gets a 'Certified Copy of Lien' letter. (6) A Notice of Intent to Garnish Wages is sent at least 30 days before the order. Garnishment needs no court order (Act 46 of 2003) and takes up to 10% of gross wages. The employer may keep 2% of the 10% as a fee. It is not released until paid in full. (7) Bank accounts can be administratively frozen and seized for liened balances. (8) After appeal rights expire and a collection notice is sent, the debt is referred to a private collection agency or outside counsel, which 'adds collection costs of up to 25 percent in addition to the amount due'. (9) Licenses and tax clearance can be denied or revoked, and the department can refer the debt to the Attorney General to take liened property.

notices: Notice of Intent to Garnish Wages
Official Notice of Wage Garnishment Termination

establishes: REV-554 lists the enforcement remedies, the 25% collection cost and the 90-day PIT appeal. The rest comes from department pages: wage garnishment (https://www.pa.gov/agencies/revenue/tax-compliance/wage-garnishment), liens (https://www.pa.gov/agencies/revenue/tax-compliance/pa-tax-liens), private collection agencies (https://www.pa.gov/agencies/revenue/tax-compliance/private-collection-agencies), notices (https://www.pa.gov/agencies/revenue/get-assistance/understanding-your-notice), and the 2025 PA-40 instructions p.24 (60-day offset notice).
uncertainty: Days between collection notices: NOT FOUND. No form numbers are published for the notices. The 25% is a maximum ('up to'), and the rate actually charged is NOT FOUND. The 2025-01-27 effective date of the 90-day window comes from search excerpts of REV-1799A and secondary firm summaries (BDO, Cozen O'Connor). REV-554 itself states the 90 days.
designImplication: PA escalation: bill (30d), assessment (90d to appeal), offset notice (60d), lien, garnishment notice (30d), 10% wage garnishment, then agency referral adding up to 25%.

claim: The department sends a Personal Income Tax Non-Filer notice based on income it has identified (Bureau of Enforcement Planning, Analysis and Discovery). If there is no reply within 30 days, the taxpayer 'will be assessed tax, interest, and penalty based on the identified unreported income'. The taxpayer can reply with a return or a signed Statement of No Liability or Previously Reported Income. By statute, when no return is filed the department 'may make an estimated assessment (based on information available)', and the tax is due within ninety days after the notice of estimated assessment is mailed, unless a petition for reassessment is filed.
establishes: The 30-day non-filer reply window. The estimated assessment and its 90-day window come from 72 P.S. 7338 (read at https://codes.findlaw.com/pa/title-72-ps-taxation-and-fiscal-affairs/pa-st-sect-72-7338/).
uncertainty: The FAQ site blocked direct fetching, so the 30-day figure and the quoted text come from search-engine excerpts of the official FAQ page. 7338 was read on FindLaw (secondary host, marked current to 2026-01-01). The non-filer notice's form number: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: A PA non-filer gets 30 days to answer, then an estimated assessment from third-party income with both penalties and interest, then 90 days to pay or appeal.

claim: When a partial payment is made against tax, penalties, interest, lien fees or other additions, the department applies it in this order: use tax (if applicable); personal income tax; interest; penalties; and legal fees.
establishes: The department's published order for applying partial PIT payments.
uncertainty: A statute or regulation setting the order: NOT FOUND. The order is the department's published practice.
designImplication: PA pays tax first, then interest before penalties. Since interest runs only on tax, paying tax first stops the growth.

claim: The PA-40 instructions list refund offsets in this order: (1) outstanding PA PIT from prior years; (2) delinquent spousal or child support, collected with DHS (a married obligor must file separately, or the refund is held); (3) court-ordered criminal obligations, through the AOPC to the county clerk of courts; (4) delinquent federal income tax, under the State Income Tax Levy Program, in which the department sends the refund to the IRS. Outbound, PA submits delinquent PIT to the federal Treasury Offset Program after a 60-day notice, and the IRS intercepts federal refunds. No PA source names a refund-offset agreement with another state. PA's 'reciprocal agreements' (IN, MD, NJ, OH, VA, WV) cover only the taxation of wages.
establishes: The PA refund offset categories, TOP participation with its 60-day notice, and the State Income Tax Levy Program that sends PA refunds to the IRS. REV-554 also lists federal refund offset as a remedy.
uncertainty: Agreements to offset refunds with other states: NOT FOUND. No PA source mentions any, and the wage reciprocity agreements are not offset agreements.
designImplication: PA refunds are offset for prior PIT, support, court debts and the IRS. Federal refunds are offset for PA debt. Do not model cross-state refund offsets for PA.

claim: For failure to pay tax when due, 'a penalty may be imposed not exceeding twice the applicable interest charged'. The ODT failure-to-file notice explainer puts it as 'Late payment penalty is double the interest rate.' The penalty is discretionary ('may') and scales with interest, so it accrues as interest does (simple, daily) and is capped at twice the interest. No minimum.
establishes: R.C. 5747.15(A) sets the late-payment penalty. The plain-language 'double the interest rate' is in the ODT ITDQ0009 explainer (https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/tax.ohio.gov/individual/FailuretoFileNotice103019.pdf), and ODT's sample Notice of Assessment (bL0006) shows it as a separate 'Late Payment Penalty' line.
uncertainty: effectiveAnnualRate_2026 (14%) is derived as 2 x 7%, not stated. On ODT's sample assessment the penalty ($430.26) is not exactly twice the pre-assessment interest shown ($243.26), so the base ODT uses in practice is uncertain.
designImplication: Model OH late payment as up to twice the interest accrued on the unpaid tax, about 14% a year in 2026.

claim: For failure to file a return, a penalty 'not exceeding the greater of fifty dollars per month or fraction of a month, not to exceed five hundred dollars, or five per cent per month or fraction of a month, not to exceed fifty per cent' of the tax. ODT says it applies 'even if the late-filed return results in a refund'. The statute sets no combined cap with the late-payment penalty. The two appear as separate lines on the assessment.
establishes: R.C. 5747.15(A) sets the late-filing penalty. The ODT failure-to-file explainer (October 2019) restates it, including that it applies when a refund is due.
uncertainty: The $50 minimum is read from the flat prong: under the greater-of rule, one month late costs at least $50. No source calls it a minimum. Combined cap: NOT FOUND (none in the statute).
designImplication: OH late filing is the greater of $50 a month (to $500) or 5% a month (to 50%), even on a refund return, on top of the late-payment penalty of twice the interest.

claim: The 2026 income tax rate is 7% a year (8% in 2024 and 2025), certified annually under R.C. 5703.47 as the federal short-term rate rounded, plus 3 points. Interest is simple and daily: tax due x rate x days late / days in year. ODT also lists a monthly accrual of 0.58% for 2026. Before assessment, interest runs on tax only, from the unextended due date until payment or assessment (R.C. 5747.08(G)). If an assessment is unpaid after 60 days, the tax portion bears interest from the assessment date. Once certified to the Attorney General, 'the entire unpaid portion of the assessment', penalties included, bears interest from certification (R.C. 5747.13(C)). ODT: interest 'cannot be waived or abated for any reason'.

value.accrual: daily (tax x rate x days / days in year)

sourceDate: page header dated 2020-03-31, content lists the 2026 rates; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: ODT gives the 2026 rate, the formula and the simple daily method. R.C. 5747.13(C), effective 2026-06-16 (https://codes.ohio.gov/assets/laws/revised-code/authenticated/57/5747/5747.13/6-16-2026/5747.13-6-16-2026.pdf), puts interest on tax only before certification and on the whole assessment after. ODT's Income Billings and Assessments FAQ #7 says interest cannot be abated.
uncertainty: None material. The page header date (2020) is when the page was created; its content lists 2026.
designImplication: Ohio: 7% simple, daily, on tax. At AG certification the base widens to tax plus penalties plus interest, a real step up in growth.

claim: ODT is not authorized to set up payment plans. It accepts partial payments, but they 'will not stop the imposition of additional interest or the referral of the account to the Attorney General's Office'. A plan is available only after the debt is certified to the Ohio Attorney General. The AG 'can accept your request for installment payments and agree to payment plans of up to one year'. The taxpayer must 'meet with a representative of the Attorney General's Office and to sign a payment contract'. By statute (R.C. 131.02(E)(2)), the AG and the agency may accept 'monthly or other periodic payments' for 'a reasonable period' and may require security.

value.collectionCostApplies: AG collection cost added at certification (see collection-sequence)

establishes: No ODT plan, and an AG plan of up to one year with a signed contract. ODT's sample Notice of Assessment (bL0006, dated April 25, 2026) repeats: 'The AGO may agree to a one-year payment plan, under certain conditions.'
uncertainty: Maximum balance: NOT FOUND. Plan-specific fee: NOT FOUND (the AG collection cost is added at certification regardless). Decision time: NOT FOUND. The AG's own collections FAQ pages (ohioattorneygeneral.gov) timed out on every fetch, so the AG terms here come from ODT pages and the statute.
designImplication: An Ohio taxpayer cannot get a plan until the debt already carries the AG collection cost. Plans last at most 12 months.

claim: No official source found states what a missed AG plan payment does, whether there is a cure period, or whether a new balance joins the plan. On refunds, ODT's offset page says Ohio law requires ODT to apply a refund to 'Taxes owed to ODT' and 'Miscellaneous debts owed to the Ohio Attorney General's office', with no exception for debts on a payment plan.
establishes: Certified debts are subject to state refund offset with no carve-out for plans.
uncertainty: Missed-payment effect, cure period, new-balance treatment: NOT FOUND. Secondary sites (taxcure.com, allstatetaxresolution.com) say the agreement defaults and enforcement resumes if a payment is missed or new returns are not filed and paid. That is not used as a value. refundsOffsetDuringPlan is inferred from the unconditional offset statute and page.
designImplication: Treat Ohio plan default mechanics as unknown. Refunds keep being offset while on an AG plan.

claim: ODT's 'debt cycle' for individual income tax has four stages. (1) Billing: a Billing Notice - Non-Remittance (bL0001) for tax plus interest, or a Notice of Adjustment. The response time is set on each notice. (2) Assessment: a Notice of Assessment (bL0006), the first legal notice, generally sent by certified mail, adds penalties. The taxpayer has 60 days after service to pay or petition for reassessment, and the assessment is final after that. A Notice of Corrected Assessment or Final Determination also carries a 60-day appeal period. (3) Post Appeal: a Post Appeal Notice (bL0008) on day 1 adds post-assessment interest. ODT's sample shows a response date 46 days after the notice date. A 'Top Notice' on day 45 says the balance will be eligible for the Treasury Offset Program in 60 days. (4) Certified: the balance is certified to the Ohio Attorney General. R.C. 131.02 requires certifying state claims unpaid 45 days after they are due, and the AG must notify the debtor. The AG 'may assess the collection cost', which R.C. 109.081 sets at up to 11% of amounts collected, 'fully recoverable from the party indebted'. A judgment lien is filed with the county clerk of courts, execution may issue (R.C. 5747.13(C)), and the AG may use private attorneys or collection agencies.

notices: Attorney General notice of certified claim
value.lien: judgment lien with county clerk of courts

sourceDate: page undated (covers notices issued since 2023-09-05); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: The ODT notice stages, letter IDs and day counts, from the notices page and the sample PDFs bL0006 (https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/tax.ohio.gov/tutorial/ADA_Notice_of_Assessment.ver1.pdf) and bL0008 (https://tax.ohio.gov/static/tutorial/post%20appeal%20notice.pdf). The AG cost cap is in R.C. 109.081 (https://codes.ohio.gov/ohio-revised-code/section-109.081, effective 2017-04-06). Certification at 45 days and the AG notice are in R.C. 131.02 (effective 2026-03-20).
uncertainty: The 10% figure (agCollectionCostReportedPct) comes only from search-engine excerpts of ohioattorneygeneral.gov FAQ pages, which timed out on direct fetch; the statute says only 'up to eleven per cent'. The wage garnishment and bank attachment procedure and amounts: NOT FOUND on official sources (secondary sites say the AG uses both). Days from billing notice to assessment: NOT FOUND (ODT: 'Response times vary').
designImplication: Ohio escalation: bill, assessment (60 days, penalties added), post-appeal notice, TOP notice at day 45 (TOP-eligible 60 days later), AG certification with up to 11% collection cost, interest on the whole balance, and a judgment lien.

claim: ODT sends an Individual Income Tax Failure to File notice (ITDQ0009), based on IRS data showing a federal return filed with an Ohio address. It reports no tax amount. It asks for a return, proof of nonresidency (or an IT 10), or proof of filing: 'Please respond within 21 days to avoid further collection actions.' The 2016 version said 20 days. Without an adequate response the bill moves to assessment. Under R.C. 5747.13(A) the commissioner may assess 'based upon any information in the commissioner's possession', with no time limit for a non-filer. A non-filer who petitions must file the IT 1040 with the petition, and must pay the assessment with it unless claiming no nexus or a liability of $1.00 or less (R.C. 5747.13(E)(3)). Penalties at assessment include the late-filing penalty.

value.assessmentBasis: any information in the commissioner's possession (IRS data)

sourceDate: ODT explainer for notices sent from 2019-10-31; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: The letter ID of the non-filer notice and its 21-day reply window. The assessment basis, the missing limitations period and the prepayment rule for a petition come from R.C. 5747.13 (effective 2026-06-16) and the bL0006 sample.
uncertainty: The 21-day figure is from a 2019 ODT explainer. Whether the 2026 ITDQ0009 still says 21 days was not confirmed; ODT's current notices page says response times vary.
designImplication: An Ohio non-filer gets about three weeks. Then comes an assessment built from IRS data with no statute of limitations, which must be prepaid to contest.

claim: No Ohio statute, rule or ODT or AG page found states the order in which a partial individual income tax payment is applied among tax, interest and penalty. ODT says only: 'We will apply partial payments to the outstanding balance.'
establishes: Only that partial payments are accepted and applied to the balance.
uncertainty: NOT FOUND. Searched R.C. 5747.08, 5747.13, 5747.15, 131.02 and Ohio Adm.Code 5703-7-05.
designImplication: Do not assume an order for Ohio. If the game needs one, flag it as a design choice, not a sourced rule.

claim: Ohio and federal law require ODT to apply a refund, including a joint refund (subject to a non-liable spouse worksheet), to: taxes owed to ODT; taxes owed to the IRS; Bureau of Workers' Compensation premiums; child or spousal support (ODJFS); public assistance overpayments (ODJFS); and 'Miscellaneous debts owed to the Ohio Attorney General's office'. The offset letter is cL0102. R.C. 5747.12 gives priority to certain trust-fund tax debts (sales tax responsible-party debts and withholding). Outbound, Ohio tax that is unpaid and unappealed 60 days after assessment may be submitted to the federal Treasury Offset Program, and it stays eligible until paid. No ODT source names a refund-offset agreement with another state. Ohio's reciprocity states (IN, KY, MI, PA, WV) cover only wage withholding.

federalTOP.eligibleAfter: 60 days after assessment if unpaid and unappealed

establishes: ODT's list of offset categories, which cites R.C. 5747.12, 5747.121 to 5747.123 and Ohio Adm.Code 5703-7-13. TOP participation is from the bL0006 sample (Treasury Offset Program Notification section) and the notices page.
uncertainty: Agreements to offset refunds with other states: NOT FOUND. A full ranking of the offset categories beyond the R.C. 5747.12 trust-fund priority: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: Ohio refunds go to state debts (including AG-certified ones) and to the IRS. Federal refunds are offset for Ohio debt. Do not model cross-state offsets for Ohio.
